$comment: THE DEPLOYMENT TOPOLOGY. This file is the single source of truth for every
hostname, Worker name, Cloudflare resource NAME and service-binding edge in
this repository. Nothing else may restate those facts, and
`tooling/scripts/check-deployment-topology.mjs` fails when they disagree.
WHY A MANIFEST. Before this file, the topology was assembled from four places
that could each be edited independently: the wrangler configs, the
`injections:` blocks in the deploy workflows, the GitHub repository
variables, and the bodies of the docs. Nothing checked them against each
other, so a hostname could change in one and not another and the pipeline
would still be green. One owner is the fix, not more places to keep in step.
WHAT IS *NOT* HERE, AND WHY. Cloudflare RESOURCE IDs are absent — and so is
any way of naming one. There is no `database_id`, no `namespace_id`, no
`resource_id`, no `$TOKEN`, no `id_env_var`, no `id_source`, and no map from
a placeholder to a GitHub variable or secret name. A D1 database and its id
are two different things: this file names the DATABASE, and the id is
rediscovered from Cloudflare by that name on every run.
The direction of truth is one-way and has no fallback:
topology.json  ->  logical name  ->  Cloudflare lookup (exact name)
->  resolved descriptor (ephemeral)
->  generated wrangler configuration
The descriptor is written to a runner's temp directory and deleted with the
job. It is never committed, never uploaded as an artefact and never stored
in GitHub. GitHub Secrets and Variables hold API tokens and nothing else —
they are not a source of truth for any identifier.
A missing id cannot happen, because nothing here carries one: there is no
default to invent and no variable to fall back to. A resource that cannot be
found by name is a deployment that stops, and stops loudly.
READ THIS BEFORE EDITING. Every field here is load-bearing for a deletion
safety property. `preview.never_delete` is the set that a cleanup run refuses
to touch even if a grammar test is wrong; `preview.grammar` is what decides
whether a discovered resource is a preview resource at all. Both are
checked, and the deletion code tests them independently of each other.
One Cloudflare account. Isolation between environments is achieved by
resource naming, bindings, the topology checker and API-token scope —
NOT by separate accounts.
This was decided, not defaulted to. The repository was previously
configured for three accounts (`STAGING_CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`,
`PRODUCTION_CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` and `ROLLBACK_CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`,
the last of which no lane named at all). Splitting by account makes
isolation the platform's job and this repository's job smaller, at the cost
of one invariant nobody can verify from a single account's state. One
account means `pnpm infra:verify` can see the whole topology and prove that
no preview resource is bound to a production one — which is the property
the preview lifecycle actually depends on.
`id` is written here, literally, and it is not an indirection. The account
id is not a generated resource id: Cloudflare does not mint it, it does not
change, and it names the account rather than anything inside it. The three
GitHub Secrets that used to carry per-lane copies of it are gone; every
workflow reads this value from this file.
It is a public identifier and is treated as one. It is a property of the
infrastructure, not a bearer credential, and hiding it would protect
nothing — the account it names is one zone and four Workers away.
Numbers, not prose, so that raising a ceiling is a diff a reviewer sees.
`custom_domains_per_zone` is the BINDING constraint, not Workers. Cloudflare
caps Workers Custom Domains at 100 per zone, and the cap is not raised by
plan. Six are consumed permanently by production and staging, and each
preview consumes `custom_domains_per_preview` of them — three: `identity`,
`identity-admin` and `home-web`. Only `identity-jobs` is private and never
gets a hostname. Twenty active previews therefore use 6 + 60 = 66 of 100,
leaving headroom for anything else this zone is later asked to host.
`max_active_previews` is what the provisioning guard enforces. The Workers
cap (500/account) is checked in the same guard but is nowhere near binding:
20 previews x 4 Workers = 80. It is recorded here so that nobody raises
`max_active_previews` on the reasoning that "workers are fine" — they are
fine, and the domain cap is what stops them.
D1 is deliberately absent. Cloudflare allows 50,000 databases per account on
the paid plan, and this repository will never approach it. Encoding a limit
that cannot bind is how a real limit later goes unnoticed.
Templates, not a vocabulary. Every name in every environment is derived from
one of these, which is what makes a preview resource predictable from a PR
number alone — and therefore findable after a crashed run, and recognisable
as ours during cleanup.
`{pr}` is the pull request number, validated against `^[1-9][0-9]*$` and
capped by `preview.max_pr_number` before it reaches any of these.
`host_prefix` is a PREFIX, not a hostname. Every host is `{host_prefix}-`,
the zone, EXCEPT the home page, which is the zone apex in production and a
prefixed subdomain everywhere else — production serves `ecoma.io`, staging
serves `stg-home.ecoma.io`, preview 123 serves `pr123-home.ecoma.io`. That
asymmetry is why these are stored as prefixes: a template that made the apex
by deleting a segment would make the preview grammar match `pr123.ecoma.io`,
which is a host this repository does not serve.
The four deployables, and which of them are reachable from the internet.
`identity-jobs` is `public: false` in every environment including preview. It
is a queue consumer: it is reached by queue messages and by no hostname. It
is also absent from the identity workers' rate-limit set and from the custom
domain budget, for the same reason.
`migrations` names the D1 database a service owns. Exactly one service has
one: SC-02 holds the Admin Worker to no identity database and SC-03 holds
the Jobs Worker to no identity state, so `identity-admin` and `identity-jobs`
cannot appear here and a check fails if they try.
Which binding slot each deployable holds, as a SLOT NAME and not a value.
The value — which database, which namespace, which Worker — is per
environment and lives under `environments`.
The service-binding lists are the security-critical part. Every one of them
points at the SAME environment's `identity` Worker, and a check fails if a
staging or preview entry names a production Worker. A preview admin Worker
that could reach production `identity` would be a complete authentication
bypass with a public URL, so this is checked mechanically rather than by
reading the generated config.
These are binding NAMES — the strings the Worker reads through `env`. They
are not Cloudflare resource ids and are not redacted by the id rules above:
`IDENTITY_DB` names a slot, and Cloudflare has never minted anything by
that name.
The locale preference cookie's NAME, per environment and per PR.
Why this is in the deployment model at all: the cookie name is a property of
where a site is deployed, not of the code. Production and staging would
otherwise share one cookie over `.ecoma.io`, and every open preview would
share another — a visitor's language preference set on one preview leaking
into all of them.
These are complete cookie names, not prefixes. The apps must set exactly
what is written here; nothing downstream appends `_locale` of its own
accord, because a name composed from two owners is a name with two owners.
This is the authentication cookie's opposite on purpose. The session cookie
`__Host-ecoma_session`
(`crates/identity-cloudflare/src/request.rs:60`) is host-only, prefixed
`__Host-` and HttpOnly, and is NOT named per environment: it cannot be read
by JavaScript and cannot be set by a sibling host, so there is nothing to
isolate. Only the non-sensitive preference cookie needs a namespace.
`cookie_prefix` under each environment is this same value, kept where the
per-environment block already carries the rest of that environment's
identity. The two are checked against each other.
A real provider. The Worker it binds to is NOT defined by this
repository — see issue #18. The binding is recorded here so the
topology is complete, and `provisioned: false` says plainly that the
target does not exist yet rather than letting a deploy discover it.
`service` names a Worker that does not exist. That is a name, not an
id, and it stays here because the deployment has to be able to name what
it wants; `provisioned: false` is what stops the claim. It used to be
`$PRODUCTION_EMAIL_PROVIDER`, resolved from a GitHub repository
variable — an indirection with no owner and nothing to fall back to.
Namespace ids are integers we choose; Cloudflare creates them implicitly
on first deploy and provides NO way to create, list or delete one. The
only rate-limits API in wrangler is the deprecated zone-level one. So
these are configuration, not provisioned resources, and the janitor
cannot clean them up — see `preview.not_deletable`.
They are the one identifier-like value in this file, and they are here
for the reason Cloudflare leaves no alternative: the namespace is a bare
integer with nothing to look up by name. See ADR-0017.
The rule that IS enforceable, and is checked: no two environments share
an id. A shared id means shared rate-limit counters, so staging load
tests would consume the production login budget and lock real users out.
These values are real and correct as written. They are not placeholders,
and a reader who assumes otherwise will try to "fix" them.

$comment_issuer_base_url: This was `https://identity-staging.ecoma.io` and is corrected here to
match the canonical staging hostname below. The two disagreed; the
hostname pattern is the authority. Tracked as issue #13's sibling.

$comment: Development binds nothing and calls nothing. The other three
environments all point at a provider Worker that does not exist yet,
so a development deploy was failing on an unresolvable service binding
for a send path that is DEFERRED everywhere.
`service: null` is an honest "there is no email service in this
environment" and the renderer omits the binding entirely. Inventing a
`identity-email-provider-development` name would put a fourth provider
in the topology for no reason.
Local only. `workers_dev: true` because a developer runs `wrangler dev`
and needs the workers.dev URL; the other three environments are `false`,
because a second undeclared public entrypoint on `identity` is exactly
what the domain topology exists to prevent.
The development Workers are named `{deployable}-development` and NOT the
bare production names the tracked configs declared. Under a single
account those names are the same resource, so `wrangler dev --remote`
against development would deploy over production `identity`. Tracked as
issue #12; the generated config carries the development name and a check
fails if it does not.
Everything below is a FUNCTION of the PR number. There are no preview
resource names in this file, only the templates they come from — which is
why a preview deployment costs zero tracked files and why a rerun after a
crash can rediscover what it already made.
`never_binds_production` is not decorative. It is checked as a
first-class property: a preview config naming `ecoma-identity-production`,
binding to the Worker `identity`, or carrying a `-production` email
provider fails before anything is created.
A preview-safe stub, never the production or staging provider. A
preview must not be able to send real email to a real user, and the
staging provider is production-like enough that this is a real
distinction rather than a nominal one.
The stub Worker does not exist yet, and creating it is a new
deployable requiring an ADR under SC-16. Until then a preview deploy
fails on this binding — which is the correct failure and must not be
worked around.
A preview rate-limit namespace id is a function of the PR number, and it
is an integer because Cloudflare requires one.
The fixed ids above are 1001/1002 (production), 2001/2002 (staging) and
3001/3002 (development). A preview id is `9{pr}0{role}`: the `9` prefix
cannot collide with any of them, and `pr` is capped at three digits by
`preview.max_pr_number` so `9` can never overflow into a fifth digit. A
PR number beyond the cap is refused rather than allowed to produce a
colliding id.
Colliding ids mean SHARED rate-limit counters, which is the specific bug
these namespaces exist to prevent: a preview hammering a login route
would consume the real budget and lock real users out.
Templates only, and never ids. A D1 database is created by name and its
`database_id` is rediscovered from `d1 list --json` on every run — never
from a previous run's job output, which is how a crashed workflow would
otherwise leave a second `-a` database behind.
The rules that govern preview resources. These are the most safety-critical
values in this file, because they are the only thing standing between a
cleanup run and production infrastructure.
What a preview resource's name may look like. A name that does not match
is not a preview resource and is never deleted, however old it is or
however the pull request turned out.
These are anchored and use `[0-9]+` rather than `\d`, and a deletion path
must compare the WHOLE name with no prefix matching — a `startsWith`
somewhere in this pipeline would eventually match `identity-production`.
`hostname` matches exactly the three hosts a preview serves: `pr{N}-home`,
`pr{N}-identity`, `pr{N}-admin`. It does NOT match `pr{N}.ecoma.io`, and
that is deliberate: production serves the zone apex, and a preview does
not, so the apex form is not a preview host and must never be treated as
one — in either direction. It is not a host this repository deletes and
not one it recognises as its own.
The PR number is capped at three digits, and the cap is a safety
mechanism rather than a resource limit. A preview rate-limit namespace id
is derived as `9{pr}0{role}` so it cannot collide with the fixed
per-environment ids; a fourth-digit PR would make that id five digits
long and push it into a range the manifest no longer controls. A
repository that reaches PR 1000 reallocates the prefix deliberately and
re-checks the collision, rather than having ids drift into each other
unnoticed.
Nothing else in the topology depends on the cap: Worker and resource
names, hostnames and the cleanup grammar are all unbounded and correct at
any PR number.
Tested as a literal set membership immediately before every delete, in
ADDITION to the grammar test. The grammar is the thing most likely to be
wrong in a way that lets something through; this list is the backstop
that does not depend on the grammar being correct.
Production and staging Workers, and the preview email stub pattern's
long-lived siblings. Nothing here is ever created by a preview and
nothing here is ever deleted by one.
The development entries are in this list because `wrangler dev --remote`
creates them and a janitor cannot tell a development Worker from a
preview one by age alone. Refusing to delete them is the cheap correct
answer: an abandoned `-development` Worker costs nothing, and deleting one
somebody is running locally breaks their next `wrangler dev --remote`.
EVERY kind in `preview.grammar` has an entry here, and the key is the
grammar's own key: `worker`, singular, like `d1`, `kv` and the rest. The
key used to read `workers` while `previewResources` called the same
resources `worker`, and `isNeverDeleted` — which asked for `worker` —
found no list and answered "not protected" for every Worker in the
account, including production. The mismatch was invisible because a
missing list and an empty one return the same thing.
A kind with grammar and no list is that same fault waiting to happen,
so `validate-topology.mjs` fails when any grammar kind is missing here.
The check is cheap and it is the only reason this can be stated as a
rule rather than as a hope.
`dlq` names three names the `queue` list also carries. That is not
redundancy to be tidied: `deletion_order` deletes the dead-letter queue
as its own step, guarded by the `dlq` list, and the `queue` list has
always covered both because a DLQ and its queue share a name prefix.
A cleanup run asks about a DLQ under `dlq`, and a caller that has only
the queue name in hand is protected by the other list.
Resources that exist, cost nothing when unused, and CANNOT be deleted
because Cloudflare provides no API for it. Listed explicitly so that a
reader does not conclude they were forgotten.
A rate-limit namespace is an integer the account remembers. It is
created implicitly the first time a Worker uses it. There is no wrangler
command to create, enumerate or delete one — the only `rate_limits`
endpoint in the API is the deprecated zone-level one. An abandoned
namespace is an integer that nothing points at, which is not a resource
leak.
What IS enforced, and is checked: no two environments may share an id,
because a shared id means shared counters.
Reverse topological, and custom domains before Workers.
Domains go first because they are the public entrypoint: a Worker that is
about to be deleted should stop answering on a public hostname first, so
there is no window in which a hostname resolves to a half-deleted Worker.
Workers go in reverse dependency order — the consumers before the thing
they consume — so no deletion orphans a live service binding. Each delete
is attempted WITHOUT `--force` first, because wrangler's force flag is
"delete even if doing so will break other Workers that depend on this
one"; letting Cloudflare refuse is how the guard is enforced rather than
re-implemented. The janitor never passes `--force` at all: a resource it
cannot delete cleanly is a resource it reports as surviving, which is the
honest outcome.
What cleanup is allowed to act on. Three states, and the third is the
point.
`unknown` means "could not establish that the PR is closed" — which
includes GitHub being unreachable. The correct action is to delete
nothing and say why. A janitor that treats an API failure as "probably
closed" will eventually delete a live preview's infrastructure, and one
that stays silent is worse than one that fails loudly.
`open` includes REOPENED. A teardown that started when a PR closed and a
reopen that arrives mid-run must not race: the delete path re-reads the
state at delete time rather than trusting the state at job start.
